# Fingerprint canonicalisation vectors — provenance

**`fingerprint.json` was not generated by this SDK, and must never be
regenerated from it.**

It is the shared cross-port fixture for the fingerprint canonicalisation rule
implemented here by `src/fingerprint.ts`, and it is the same file all eight
Tamga SDKs test against. Its digests were produced by an independent SHA-256
implementation. They were re-verified against Node's own `node:crypto` before
this port was written, so the algorithm was pinned before any of this repo's
code existed to agree with.

## Why this matters

This repo has already shipped the failure mode this rule exists to prevent.
`test/helpers/checkoutFixtures.ts` made the same ECDSA mistake on the *signing*
side that `src/crypto/ecdsa.ts` made on the *verifying* side, so the round trip
was green while no server-issued ECDSA machine file could be verified. A fixture
an SDK produced can only ever prove that the SDK agrees with itself.

**Do not add a vector computed by this repository to this file.** If a case is
missing, have it produced by an implementation that is not this one, and add it
to the shared fixture rather than to a copy.

## Reading it

`_spec` states the algorithm and every validation rule, including why Unicode
normalisation is deliberately absent. Read it before changing anything here.

`canonical` writes the U+001F unit separator as the display placeholder `<US>`.
The real byte is what gets hashed; `test/fingerprint.spec.ts` substitutes it
back before comparing.

`vectors` are inputs that must succeed, each with both its canonical string and
its digest — the canonical string is what localises a disagreement, the digest
is what proves agreement. `rejected` are inputs that must throw. Both arrays are
iterated, and the spec asserts their lengths, so a vector added to this file is
exercised without a test edit and a vector *removed* from it fails loudly rather
than silently reducing coverage.

## The traps these vectors pin

Three pairs matter most, and each is a pair on purpose:

- `two_sorted` / `two_unsorted` — the same components in different caller order
  must produce the same fingerprint. Ordering is the caller's convenience, not
  part of the machine's identity.
- `whitespace_trimmed` / `single` — must be equal. A value read from a file, a
  command's stdout or an environment variable arrives with a trailing newline
  nobody sees, and that newline was previously a second seat.
- `case_preserved` / `single` — must **not** be equal. Case folding is absent on
  purpose: lowercasing a base64 or hex identifier corrupts it.

`non_ascii_value` pins that values pass through as their UTF-8 bytes with **no**
Unicode normalisation. JavaScript has `String.prototype.normalize` built in, so
this is the one port where adding NFC would look free — and that is exactly why
the rule is written down here. NFC needs a new dependency in Rust and Go and
either ICU or hand-rolled Unicode tables in C11. A rule eight ports cannot
implement identically would produce two fingerprints for one machine depending
on which SDK the application was written with.
